question: What other systems, besides photonic crystals, have demonstrated bound states in the continuum?

ingredients.name: answer_critical_0
ingredients.criterion: Answer identifies slab-on-substrate phononic crystals as a non-photonic-crystal system demonstrating mechanical BICs (symmetry-induced and accidental, with topological charges), trapping phonons without coupling into the substrate regardless of acoustic impedance mismatch.
examples: mechanical BICs realized in unreleased slab-on-substrate phononic crystals
phonon trapping in the continuum irrespective of slab/substrate impedance
symmetry-induced and accidental mechanical BICs with topological charges
radiation loss eliminated by introducing voids at the PnC boundary

ingredients.name: answer_critical_1
ingredients.criterion: Answer identifies individual optomechanical microresonators (e.g., wheel-shaped) as a platform where a Friedrich–Wintgen mechanical BIC was experimentally realized via azimuthal-symmetry breaking, coupling two dissipative modes for destructive interference and zero clamping loss.
examples: BIC in a wheel-shaped optomechanical microresonator with broken azimuthal symmetry
destructive interference between dissipation channels of two mechanical modes
zero clamping loss with mechanical Q ~10^4 in the very high frequency band at room temperature

ingredients.name: answer_critical_2
ingredients.criterion: Answer identifies open acoustic resonators (2D and 3D, e.g., cylindrical cavities coaxially connected to semi-infinite waveguides) as systems demonstrating BICs via collapse of Fano resonances, where two degenerate same-symmetry modes destructively interfere to form an embedded trapped mode.
examples: cylindrical acoustic resonators coaxially connected to semi-infinite waveguides
embedded trapped mode from full destructive interference of two degenerate same-symmetry modes
singular points where unit and zero transmittance coalesce (Fano-resonance collapse)
tuning degeneracy points by varying resonator length

ingredients.name: answer_critical_3
ingredients.criterion: Answer distinguishes the trapping mechanisms across systems: symmetry-based protection (symmetry mismatch with the radiation continuum) versus interference-based Friedrich–Wintgen trapping (destructive interference between dissipation channels or degenerate modes), correctly attributed to the appropriate systems.
examples: symmetry-induced BICs protected by symmetry mismatch with the radiation channel
Friedrich–Wintgen BIC from coupling two dissipative modes so radiation destructively interferes
accidental mechanical BICs tuned by parameter variation
acoustic coupled mode theory used to analyze the BICs

ingredients.name: answer_critical_4
ingredients.criterion: Answer enumerates at least two distinct non-photonic-crystal domains (mechanical/phononic and acoustic), framing BICs as demonstrated/proposed across multiple physical systems rather than giving a single example.
examples: BICs studied in phononic, optomechanical, and acoustic platforms
mechanical BICs in PnCs and microresonators plus acoustic BICs in open resonators
in addition to photonic crystals, BICs appear in mechanical and acoustic systems

ingredients.name: valuable_0
ingredients.criterion: Answer distinguishes experimentally demonstrated systems (phononic crystals, optomechanical microresonators) from theoretically proposed ones (open acoustic resonators, with tuning speculated via piston-like hollow-stem waveguides), and may note prior microwave realizations of the Friedrich–Wintgen mechanism.
examples: mechanical BICs experimentally realized in PnCs and microresonators
acoustic resonator BIC tuning speculated via piston-like hollow-stem waveguides
Friedrich–Wintgen mechanism previously experimentally realized only in microwave set-ups (e.g., Lepetit et al.)
degeneracy points accessed parametrically by varying resonator length

ingredients.name: valuable_1
ingredients.criterion: Answer notes applications enabled by these BIC systems (electromechanics, optomechanics, quantum physics, high-Q resonators, noninvasive optical interrogation of trapped phonons) and practical benefits such as robust devices with large supporting structures and reduced fabrication difficulty, contrasting with conventional bandgap engineering or minimized-support approaches.
examples: high-Q micro/nanomechanical resonators with robust supporting structures
applications in electromechanics, optomechanics, and quantum physics
supporting rod widths up to 5 μm, defying fragile-device convention
zero-wavevector BIC phonons coupling to optical resonances for noninvasive interrogation
distinct from mechanical bandgap engineering in suspended structures

ingredients.name: valuable_2
ingredients.criterion: Answer mentions topological charges or features associated with the mechanical BICs in phononic crystals.
examples: BICs carrying topological charges
symmetry-induced and accidental mechanical BICs with topological features
